title: European Nations State Their Vision for the Future of European Security
gist: Commentary on the non-binding 'Declaration on key principles of European security' signed by 40 European states at the EPC Summit in Dublin: Europe rejects Russia's spheres-of-influence model, insists on a seat at any US-Russia negotiation, and pairs posture-building (strength) with limited risk-reduction norms rather than early arms control that could lock in capability gaps.

insights.claim: Forty European countries signed a non-binding 'Declaration on key principles of European security' at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, setting out 10 principles and 13 common objectives, with only seven EPC members (including Serbia and Switzerland) withholding signature.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Broad European cohesion on Ukraine reduces the odds of a US-Russia deal imposed over European heads.

insights.claim: Because such a declaration takes weeks to prepare, it was likely not triggered by the Abu Dhabi talks but reflects work France, Germany and the UK began earlier, as Macron described in his March 2026 Île longue speech.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: European security framework planning is a structured, ongoing E3-led process, not a reactive one.

insights.claim: The declaration states that any matter affecting European security should be decided with Europeans, backed by real leverage since Europe controls capability development, arms for Ukraine, EU membership and sanctions.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Sanctions and EU accession are bargaining chips Europe can withhold, so any Ukraine settlement needs European buy-in to stick.
insights.quote: any matter affecting European security should be decided with the Europeans
insights.locator: European States Will Not Accept Being Circumvented

insights.claim: Russia is calculating that the Trump administration's desire to end the Ukraine war and avoid escalation could lead it to accept wider Russian claims on Europe, either by pressuring Europeans or via levers like US deployments and the Force Posture Review.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Watch US force-posture announcements in Europe as a signal of whether Washington is trading European security for a Ukraine deal.

insights.claim: Russia's late-2021 draft agreements sought to end NATO nuclear sharing, bar NATO enlargement and forbid foreign deployments on territories of states that joined NATO after 1997, creating zones of differentiated security.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: These remain the template for Russia's maximalist demands; any reappearance in negotiations is a red flag for eastern-flank security.

insights.claim: Accepting Russia's wider demands would not serve US interests because weakening NATO deterrence raises the risk of a Russian 'test' triggering Article 5, which would reabsorb the US resources burden shifting aims to free for the Indo-Pacific.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Argues US Indo-Pacific pivot depends on a strong, sequenced European handover rather than a rushed drawdown.
insights.quote: a prerequisite is to prevent an Article 5 circumstance, because that would reabsorb U.S. resources
insights.locator: It seems it would not be

insights.claim: NATO burden shifting should occur in a planned and sequenced manner so that the overall deterrence and defense posture in Europe is not weakened during the transition.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Sequencing implies gradual US withdrawals matched to European capability ramp, sustaining multi-year European defense procurement.

insights.claim: Security rests on two complementary tracks, strength to deter and defend and norms to regulate competition, mirroring NATO's 1979 dual-track approach that combined Euromissile deployments with negotiations leading to the INF Treaty.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Expect European rearmament to come first, with negotiation tracks lagging behind capability build-out.
insights.quote: Norms without strength to back them up would not be credible.

insights.claim: European states' current priority is reinforcing posture and closing capability gaps with Russia, pursued through defragmenting cooperation: a stronger defense industrial base, joint capabilities, joint planning and resilience against sub-threshold aggression.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Supports sustained demand for European defense industry and joint procurement programs.

insights.claim: Ukraine's signature of the first common objective carries signal weight because, as an EU candidate, it is among those referencing frameworks including the Treaty on European Union's mutual assistance clause.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Strengthens Ukraine's political integration into European security commitments short of NATO membership.

insights.claim: Signatories support discussions on risk management and reduction mechanisms with Russia only once conditions are met and peace is restored, preferring measures like exercise notifications and communication channels that treat armament levels as given.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Post-war Europe-Russia talks are likely to focus on de-confliction, not weapons caps, so rearmament budgets are unlikely to be negotiated away.

insights.claim: Moving too early into arms control could lock in Europe's capability gaps with Russia and let Russia create new gaps by violating commitments, as it did with the INF Treaty.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Explains why European governments will resist early arms-control proposals that would constrain procurement.
insights.quote: if European states went too early into arms control, they could “lock in” the capability gaps

insights.claim: European unity may fracture as frontline states most exposed to Russia resist even risk-management talks, and any move toward trades or concessions would expose divergent strategic interests.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Watch eastern-flank states (most exposed) as potential spoilers of any European negotiating position.

insights.claim: The June failure of the Franco-German Future Combat Air System illustrates the difficulty of deepening European defense industrial cooperation, and Europe risks spending more without truly increasing autonomy.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Higher European defense budgets do not guarantee pan-European programs; national champions may capture spending instead.

insights.claim: The Ukraine war has backfired on Russia by making European nations more proactive and assertive on their own security framework than in the past.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Structural European defense autonomy push is likely durable beyond any ceasefire.
insights.quote: one more way in which the Ukraine war backfired on Russia
